t: Claims expenses that can be directly attributed to a specific claim, such as surveyor's fees and legal costs, are called:
o: Management expenses
Unallocated loss adjustment expenses (ULAE)
Allocated loss adjustment expenses (ALAE)
Acquisition costs
e: ALAE are charged to the individual claim file; ULAE are general claims department overheads that cannot be tied to one claim.

t: A general insurer reports net earned premium of ₹400 crore, net incurred claims of ₹300 crore and management expenses plus commission of ₹120 crore. Its combined ratio is:
e: Combined ratio = (300 + 120)/400 = 105%; being above 100% the insurer has an underwriting loss of 5% of premium before investment income.

t: Soon after registering a claim, the insurer creates a 'case reserve'. This is:
o: An estimate of the amount the insurer expects to pay on that claim, set aside in the books until settlement
A deposit the insured must pay before the claim is processed
The surveyor's fee payable in advance
A fine imposed by IRDAI for late registration
e: Setting an initial reserve on registration ensures that outstanding claims liabilities are recognised promptly and reinsurers can be notified.

t: When an insurer writes to a claimant 'without prejudice', the purpose is to:
o: Reject the claim finally and close the file
Make an offer or communication that cannot later be used as an admission of liability
Inform the claimant that a surveyor has been appointed
Confirm that liability is admitted in full
e: Without-prejudice correspondence protects the insurer's position while negotiating; it is neither a repudiation nor an admission.

t: A claim is intimated 45 days after a burglary, the policy requiring immediate notice. The insured explains that he was hospitalised throughout. In the current regulatory climate the insurer should:
o: Reject the claim outright, since the condition is a condition precedent
Refer the claim to the police for investigation of the insured
Examine whether the delay actually prejudiced its position before invoking the condition, rather than rejecting the claim mechanically for delay
Pay only 25% of the loss as a non-standard claim
e: IRDAI and courts expect insurers to consider genuine reasons for delay; technical rejection for delay alone, where the loss is otherwise proved, is discouraged.

t: Recovery actions available to an insurer after paying a property claim include:
o: Recovery of the claim amount from the insured's bank
Deduction of the claim from the agent's commission
Recovery from the Insurance Ombudsman's fund
Sale of salvage, subrogation against the responsible third party and recovery from reinsurers
e: Salvage, subrogation and reinsurance recoveries reduce the net cost of claims; the insured, agent and Ombudsman bear no such liability.

t: In a marine cargo claim for shortage or damage, the insured must produce evidence that a claim was lodged against the carrier because:
o: The insurer's right of subrogation against the carrier must be preserved and the carrier's liability under the contract of carriage must not be time-barred
IRDAI requires carriers to co-insure all cargo policies
The carrier is the only party liable for the loss and the insurer pays nothing
The policy excludes all losses in transit unless the carrier admits liability
e: Failure to hold the carrier liable in time prejudices recovery; the insurer may reduce the claim to the extent its subrogation rights were lost.

topic: Special Features in Claims (Motor, Marine and Miscellaneous)
t: Under Section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended in 2019), the no-fault compensation payable for death in a motor accident is:
o: ₹2 lakh
₹5 lakh
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 164 fixes ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt without proof of negligence; ₹2 lakh is the hit-and-run amount under Section 161.

t: In a personal accident death claim, which document is NOT normally required?
o: Discharge summary of the hospital where the deceased was never admitted
FIR or police report relating to the accident
Post-mortem report where the death was unnatural
Death certificate issued by the registrar
e: Death certificate, post-mortem and police papers establish the fact and accidental nature of death; a discharge summary is relevant only where there was hospitalisation.

t: A 'claim bill' in a marine cargo claim is:
o: The insured's computation of the amount claimed, showing insured value, extent of loss and amount due
The customs duty demand on the imported goods
The carrier's bill for freight charges
The invoice raised by the surveyor for his fees
e: The claim bill summarises the claim quantum derived from the invoice, policy value and survey findings; the other options are unrelated documents.

t: Which of the following is a duty of a licensed surveyor under the IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations?
o: Deciding finally whether the insurer is liable to pay the claim
Issuing the discharge voucher and making payment to the insured
Collecting the premium from the insured on behalf of the insurer
Investigating the cause and circumstances of the loss, assessing its extent and advising on salvage and subrogation
e: The surveyor assesses and reports; admission of liability, payment and discharge remain the insurer's functions.

t: After receiving the final survey report, the insurer must decide on the claim within how many days under the 2024 IRDAI protection of policyholders' interests regulations?
o: 30 days
15 days
7 days
45 days
e: The 2024 regulations require a decision within 7 days of the survey report; the surveyor in turn has 15 days from appointment to submit the report.

t: A 'joint survey' in a cargo claim is one conducted:
o: By two surveyors appointed by the insurer for high-value claims
By the surveyor in the presence of representatives of the consignee and the carrier so that the extent of damage on delivery is agreed
By the insurer and the reinsurer together
By the IRDAI and the General Insurance Council
e: A joint survey with the carrier fixes the condition of goods at the time of delivery, supporting both the claim and the subsequent recovery from the carrier.

t: Membership of which body is a prerequisite for the grant and renewal of a surveyor's licence by IRDAI?
o: General Insurance Council
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
Indian Institute of Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors (IIISLA)
Insurance Institute of India (III)
e: The 2015 regulations make IIISLA membership mandatory for surveyors, with the Institute overseeing professional conduct and continuing education.

t: Which of the following policies is NOT subject to the strict principle of indemnity?
o: Personal accident policy paying a fixed capital sum
Standard fire policy on stocks
Motor own-damage policy
Marine cargo policy
e: Personal accident (like life) is a benefit policy paying agreed sums; property and marine policies indemnify the actual measurable loss.

t: A valued policy (such as a marine hull policy) differs from an unvalued policy in that:
o: Premium is payable only after the loss
Cover is restricted to total loss only
The value of the subject matter is agreed at inception and is conclusive between the parties for total loss, absent fraud
The insurer may revalue the property at the time of claim
e: In a valued policy the agreed value is the measure of indemnity, avoiding valuation disputes; an unvalued policy requires proof of value at the time of loss.

t: A building 10 years old is destroyed by fire. Its replacement cost new is ₹20 lakh and depreciation for age and use is assessed at 40%. On an indemnity (market value) basis the insured is entitled to:
o: ₹20 lakh
₹12 lakh
₹16 lakh
₹8 lakh
e: Market value = replacement cost less depreciation = 20 − 8 = ₹12 lakh; the full ₹20 lakh would be payable only under a reinstatement value clause after actual reinstatement.

t: The doctrine of proximate cause requires the claims official to identify:
o: The cause that is most convenient for the insured
The dominant, effective cause that set the chain of events in motion leading to the loss
Every remote cause contributing to the loss
The last event in time before the loss occurred
e: Proximate cause is the active, efficient cause, not necessarily the nearest in time; the claim is admissible if that cause is an insured peril.

t: In a fire policy, the in-built cover for removal of debris under the Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy is limited to:
o: 1% of the claim amount
10% of the claim amount
₹1 lakh in all cases
5% of the sum insured
e: Debris removal up to 1% of the claim amount is built in; a higher limit must be separately insured by add-on.

t: A motor accident claim under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is decided by:
o: The Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal
The District Consumer Commission
The IRDAI
The Insurance Ombudsman
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). MACTs have exclusive jurisdiction over third-party compensation claims; appeals lie to the High Court.

t: A stocks declaration policy is appropriate where:
o: Only finished goods and not raw materials are to be covered
The value of stocks fluctuates widely during the year and the insured declares monthly values, with premium adjusted at year end
The insured wants cover for stock in transit only
The stock is of constant value throughout the year
e: Declaration policies charge a provisional premium on the maximum sum insured and adjust it on the average of the declarations, suiting fluctuating stock values.

t: In assessing a stock loss after a fire, a surveyor compares the book stock with the physical salvage. The 'book stock' is derived from:
o: Opening stock plus purchases less cost of goods sold, supported by stock registers and accounts
The surveyor's estimate of the salvage value
The sum insured shown in the policy
The insured's income tax return of the previous year
e: Reconstructing stock from accounts (the trading account method) is the standard way to establish the quantity at risk when physical verification is impossible.

t: A warehouse fire damages goods worth ₹5 lakh. The salvage is sold for ₹80,000 and the surveyor allows ₹20,000 for reasonable expenses incurred in protecting salvage. The net assessed loss is:
e: Loss = 5,00,000 − 80,000 (salvage realised) + 20,000 (salvage protection expenses, which are admissible) = ₹4,40,000.

topic: Special Features of Property Damage Claims
t: Under the Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha policy, underinsurance is waived if the sum insured is not less than:
o: 50% of the value at risk
90% of the value at risk
85% of the value at risk (waiver up to 15%)
100% of the value at risk
e: BSUS applies a waiver of underinsurance up to 15%; only if the shortfall exceeds 15% does the condition of average bite, unlike SFSP where it applies fully.

t: A factory building valued at ₹50 lakh is insured for ₹40 lakh under a fire policy subject to the condition of average. A fire causes damage of ₹10 lakh. The insurer's liability (ignoring excess) is:
o: ₹8 lakh
₹10 lakh
₹4 lakh
₹6 lakh
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Under pro rata average: loss × SI / value at risk = 10 × 40/50 = ₹8 lakh; the insured bears the balance as his own insurer for the uninsured 20%.

topic: Special Features of Property Damage Claims
t: Under a fire loss of profits policy, 'gross profit' for the purpose of insurance is:
o: Sales less purchases only
Total turnover of the business
Net profit plus insured standing charges (or turnover less opening stock and uninsured working expenses, adjusted for closing stock)
Net profit after tax
e: The insurance definition of gross profit captures the net profit plus the fixed charges that continue during interruption; it is not the accountant's gross profit.

topic: Special Features of Property Damage Claims
t: A business interruption policy has a rate of gross profit of 25%. Following a fire, turnover falls by ₹40 lakh during the indemnity period and the insured spends ₹3 lakh on increased cost of working which avoided a further ₹20 lakh loss of turnover. The admissible claim (before average) is:
o: ₹8 lakh
₹18 lakh
₹13 lakh
₹10 lakh
e: Loss of gross profit = 25% × 40 = ₹10 lakh; ICW of ₹3 lakh is allowed as it is less than the gross profit saved (25% × 20 = ₹5 lakh), giving ₹13 lakh.

topic: Special Features of Property Damage Claims
t: A contractor's all risks (CAR) policy typically excludes:
o: Theft of construction materials from the site
Loss or damage due to faulty design, defective material or workmanship (except resultant damage where covered)
Collapse of partly completed works due to storm
Fire and explosion at the project site
e: CAR covers accidental physical damage to works, but the cost of rectifying inherent defects of design or workmanship is excluded.

topic: Special Features of Insurance of Persons
t: As per the IRDAI master circular on health insurance (2024), an insurer must decide on a cashless authorisation request within:
o: 7 days of receipt of the request
24 hours of receipt of the request
1 hour of receipt of the request
3 hours of receipt of the request
e: Cashless authorisation must be given within 1 hour and final discharge authorisation within 3 hours of the hospital's request; otherwise the insurer bears any extra hospital charges.

topic: Special Features of Insurance of Persons
t: After how many years of continuous coverage can a health insurer no longer contest a claim on the ground of non-disclosure or misrepresentation (except fraud)?
o: 36 months (3 years)
96 months (8 years)
24 months (2 years)
60 months (5 years)
e: The moratorium period was reduced from 8 to 5 years in 2024; after 60 months of continuous cover a claim can be contested only for established fraud.

topic: Special Features of Insurance of Persons
t: A personal accident policy provides a weekly benefit for temporary total disablement. The usual basis of this benefit is:
o: Actual medical expenses incurred without limit
1% of the capital sum insured per week, subject to a maximum number of weeks (commonly 100) and a weekly cap
50% of the capital sum insured per month
100% of the capital sum insured paid in a lump sum
e: TTD is a weekly income benefit for the period the insured is totally unable to work, capped by weeks and amount; lump-sum percentages apply to death and permanent disablement.

t: Under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, compensation for permanent total disablement is:
o: A fixed sum of ₹2 lakh
Half-monthly wages for a maximum of five years
50% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor, or ₹1,20,000, whichever is more
60% of monthly wages multiplied by the relevant factor, or ₹1,40,000, whichever is more
e: PTD attracts 60% × wages × factor with a floor of ₹1,40,000; 50%/₹1,20,000 applies to death and half-monthly payments to temporary disablement.

t: The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 makes it compulsory for owners handling hazardous substances to:
o: Insure their employees under the Employees' Compensation Act
Deposit ₹1 crore with the Pollution Control Board
Take out a professional indemnity policy
Take out insurance to provide immediate no-fault relief to victims of accidents involving the hazardous substance
e: The Act imposes no-fault liability and compulsory insurance (with a matching contribution to the Environment Relief Fund) so that victims receive relief quickly.

t: In a professional indemnity policy, the 'retroactive date' is:
o: The date on which the premium was paid
The date before which acts, errors or omissions are not covered even if the claim is made during the policy period
The date of expiry of the policy
The date on which the claim must be reported to the insurer
e: Claims-made policies cover claims made during the period arising from acts after the retroactive date, usually the date continuous cover first began.

topic: Special Features in Claims (Motor, Marine and Miscellaneous)
t: A private car with an IDV of ₹6 lakh meets with an accident. The surveyor estimates repair costs at ₹4.8 lakh. As per standard motor practice the insurer would treat this claim as:
o: A partial loss, paying ₹4.8 lakh less depreciation
A cash loss limited to 50% of the IDV
A repudiation, since the damage is excessive
A total loss / constructive total loss, since repair cost exceeds 75% of the IDV
e: Where the aggregate repair cost exceeds 75% of IDV the vehicle is treated as a total loss and settled at IDV less excess, the wreck being taken over by the insurer.

topic: Special Features in Claims (Motor, Marine and Miscellaneous)
t: Under Section 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, an insurer's liability for third-party property damage under an 'Act only' policy is limited to:
o: ₹1 lakh
Unlimited
₹7.5 lakh
e: Liability for death or bodily injury of third parties is unlimited, but TPPD under the statutory cover is capped at ₹7.5 lakh unless a higher limit is opted.

t: Section 64VB of the Insurance Act 1938 requires that:
o: Premium is received in advance before the risk is assumed
Every policy carries a free-look clause
Claims are settled within 30 days
Agents hold a valid licence
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). No risk may be assumed unless the premium has been received in advance or is guaranteed in the manner prescribed.

topic: Special Features in Claims (Motor, Marine and Miscellaneous)
t: A deceased aged 32 earned ₹30,000 per month in a permanent job and leaves a wife and two children. Applying Sarla Verma (multiplier 16) and Pranay Sethi (50% future prospects, one-third deduction for personal expenses), the loss of dependency is:
o: ₹43.2 lakh
₹86.4 lakh
₹38.4 lakh
₹57.6 lakh
e: Income with prospects = 30,000 × 1.5 = 45,000; less one-third = 30,000 per month = ₹3.6 lakh p.a.; × 16 = ₹57.6 lakh, to which conventional heads are added.

topic: Speed and Quality in Settlement of Claims
t: Which of the following practices is MOST likely to improve the speed of claim settlement without compromising quality?
o: Appointing two surveyors for every claim above ₹10,000
Fixing clear service standards, simplified documentation and delegated authority at the operating office
Requiring head office approval for every claim irrespective of size
Insisting on original documents even where digital copies are permitted
e: Service standards and delegation remove bottlenecks; centralised approvals and duplicate surveys add cost and time.

topic: Speed and Quality in Settlement of Claims
t: The IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) regulations require that a claim rejection letter must:
o: Offer a minimum ex gratia payment of 10% of the claim
Be signed by the surveyor who assessed the loss
Be issued only after approval of the Ombudsman
State the specific reasons for rejection and inform the claimant of the grievance redressal mechanism available
e: A speaking repudiation letter with reasons and details of the grievance route is mandatory; the other options have no regulatory basis.

topic: Speed and Quality in Settlement of Claims
t: Interest for delayed settlement of a claim under IRDAI regulations is payable:
o: From the date the claim ought to have been settled as per the regulatory timeline until the date of actual payment
From the date of loss until the date of claim intimation
From the date of policy inception
Only if the policyholder makes a written demand
e: Interest at bank rate plus 2% runs from the date by which the claim should have been settled; it is payable suo motu, not on demand.

t: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (as modified by the 2021 rules), a District Commission can entertain complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed:
o: ₹20 lakh
₹2 crore
₹50 lakh
₹1 crore
e: District Commissions hear claims up to ₹50 lakh, State Commissions up to ₹2 crore and the National Commission above ₹2 crore.

t: Nomination and assignment of a life insurance policy are governed respectively by which sections of the Insurance Act 1938?
o: Sections 39 and 38
Sections 38 and 39
Sections 41 and 45
Sections 45 and 41
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 39 deals with nomination; Section 38 with assignment and transfer.

t: A complaint to the Insurance Ombudsman must ordinarily be made within:
o: One year of the insurer's final rejection or of the insurer failing to reply within 30 days of the representation
Two years of the claim intimation
Three months of the date of loss
Six months of the policy expiry
e: The Ombudsman Rules require prior representation to the insurer and filing within one year of the final reply (or the expiry of 30 days without reply).

t: Following an IRDAI direction of 2023 on arbitration clauses in general insurance policies:
o: Retail (individual) policies no longer contain an arbitration clause, which is permitted only in commercial lines
The Ombudsman acts as sole arbitrator in all disputes
Arbitration now extends to disputes on liability as well as quantum
All policies must compulsorily contain an arbitration clause
e: IRDAI removed arbitration from retail policies so that individuals can approach the Ombudsman or consumer forums; commercial policyholders may still agree to arbitration.

t: 'Soft fraud' in insurance claims typically refers to:
o: Inflating or padding an otherwise genuine claim, such as including undamaged items or exaggerated bills
Staging an accident or arson to create a loss that never genuinely occurred
Impersonating an insurer's employee to collect premium
Hacking into the insurer's claims system
e: Soft fraud exaggerates real losses; hard fraud fabricates the loss altogether (staged theft, arson, fake accidents).

t: An insurer's net claims paid in a year are ₹300 crore, outstanding claims at the beginning of the year ₹100 crore and at the end ₹120 crore. Net incurred claims for the year are:
o: ₹280 crore
₹300 crore
₹520 crore
₹320 crore
e: Incurred claims = paid + closing outstanding − opening outstanding = 300 + 120 − 100 = ₹320 crore (including any IBNR movement).

t: Under the Bornhuetter-Ferguson method, with net earned premium of ₹10 crore, an expected loss ratio of 70% and 40% of ultimate claims estimated to be still unreported, the IBNR reserve is:
o: ₹7 crore
₹2.8 crore
₹4 crore
₹4.2 crore
e: Expected ultimate = 70% × 10 = ₹7 crore; IBNR = unreported proportion × expected ultimate = 40% × 7 = ₹2.8 crore, independent of the claims reported so far.

t: Video or photo-based remote survey of motor damage through a mobile app is used primarily to:
o: Replace the FIR in theft claims
Transfer the assessment responsibility to the insured
Eliminate the need for a repairer's estimate
Reduce the time and cost of physical inspection for small and medium claims while keeping an evidentiary record
e: Remote survey tools speed up low-value claims and create timestamped evidence; the assessment is still done by the insurer or surveyor.

t: IRDAI requires claim payments to policyholders to be made:
o: Through the agent who sold the policy
In cash where the claim is below ₹10,000
Through electronic modes such as NEFT/RTGS/IMPS directly to the claimant's bank account
Only by account-payee cheque
e: Electronic payment ensures traceability and speed and reduces fraud; cash and payments routed through intermediaries are not permitted.
